how: In Vietnam in 1970–71, almost half of US Army enlisted men tried narcotics, mostly heroin or opium. 20 in 100 said they'd been addicted there.
Back home, many used again without getting addicted again. Among men who used heroin often, about half got addicted again.
Treatment wasn't the reason, the lead researcher says. Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home. Those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.
These are the men's own reports, checked against military records and urine tests. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture, whose text and graphs don't always match.

fields.but: No study we read measured how much pills with the same logo differ. And the online check is one Dutch study of two websites.
how: Staff of the Dutch testing service compared 471 online reports about ecstasy pills from 2014–15 with lab results for other pills matching each description. About 40 in 100 said over 10 mg too much MDMA, 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little, and 16 in 100 missed another drug.

The authors called 15 in 100 reports dangerous: they said far too little MDMA, or left a drug out. Saying too much wasn't counted. Reports with a photo less often matched several different pills, but weren't less often dangerous. Reports giving a range were dangerous less often: 12 against 21 in 100.

The same testers say pills that looked like ecstasy, with similar logos, have held 2C-B or amphetamine. They identify some pills by exact size, weight, logo and a colour test, against pills tested in recent weeks. They call it 99% reliable but have published no data.

In lab tests of Dutch pills sold as ecstasy from 1993 to 2008, only MDMA was found in 44 in 100 in 1997 and about 86 in 100 in 2000–04. Single pills held from a trace to 225 mg. These are lab amounts, not amounts to take.

fields.but: These were overdoses, often with other pills too. For normal doses, the studies we read have only reports of seizures, not how often they happen.
how: At one Australian hospital unit, 8 of 71 people treated for a tramadol overdose had seizures. That was 2 of the 20 who took only tramadol, and 6 of the 51 who took other pills too. Seizures came up to almost a day later.

18 in 100 had breathing trouble with low oxygen, and 5 went into a coma (3 of them had also taken an older type of antidepressant). Those who said they took more had more seizures and breathing trouble, but this doesn't show that smaller amounts are safe. Nobody died.
No one met the criteria for serotonin syndrome. With 71 people, that only rules out rates above about 5 in 100. Earlier reported cases mostly involved tramadol taken with antidepressants.
In 23 Iranian hospital studies, about 35 in 100 had seizures, but single studies ranged from 12 to 69 in 100. About 7 in 1,000 died in hospital; one study had 100 in 1,000.

fields.but: Most reports describe one or a few people, or a medicine added to urine in a lab. For most medicines, we don't know how often it happens.
how: Quick screens use antibodies, which can also grab other molecules, even some that don't look like the drug. Reviews name sertraline for benzo tests. They name bupropion and pseudoephedrine for amphetamine tests, and some antibiotics for opiate tests.

The reviews give only a few numbers. In two studies of patient records, 41 in 100 unconfirmed amphetamine screens came from people taking bupropion, and about 27 in 100 unconfirmed benzo screens were linked to sertraline.

Some medicines give true positives, because they are or become the drug tested. Examples: prescribed amphetamines, prescribed THC, and codeine, which turns into morphine. There is no evidence that amoxicillin trips a cocaine test. Numbing drugs like lidocaine do not.
Both reviews say a screen is only a first step. A different lab method should check it before a big decision, like a job or a court case.
